plain: Makes a copy of the text with the first letter big and every other letter small.
Counts how many times a value shows up in a list, like tally marks in math class. A value that isn't in the list counts 0.
Reads a key without stopping. `hero.get("glug", 0)` gives the value, or 0 when the key is missing, instead of a KeyError.
Puts a new item into a list at a position. You give the position first, then the value. Each item after it moves back one place, like people in a line when a friend steps in.
The dot means: ask this text to do something. `.lower()` gives a copy in small letters. The text in the box does not change.
Takes the last item off a list and hands it back, so you can keep it in a variable. The list gets one shorter. `.pop(0)` takes the first item instead.
Takes a value out of a list: the first item that is the same as the value you hand it. You give the value, not its position. If the value isn't in the list, Python stops with a ValueError.
Joins two yes-or-no questions. The answer is `True` only when both answers are `True`, like *homework done and room clean*.
Adds one item to the end of a list, the way an appendix goes at the end of a book. It changes the list itself and hands back nothing.
What you hand over when you call a recipe. In `wave("Pip")`, the argument is `"Pip"`.
A line that says what must be true at that spot. If it is true, nothing happens. If it is not, Python stops with `AssertionError`.
`>=` means *at least*, like ≥ in math class: the number itself counts. `<=` means *at most*, like ≤. `>` and `<` leave the number itself out.
The error Python shows when a dot asks for something that isn't there. Read a dictionary with square brackets, never a dot: `hero["mana"]`, not `hero.mana`.
The indented lines under an `if`, `elif` or `else` line, like the sub-points under one main point in an outline. They run together, or not at all.
One of the paths Python can take: the lines under the `if`, under one `elif`, or under the `else`. Python takes only one of them.
A mistake in code. A loud bug stops Python with an error. A quiet bug runs, but gives a wrong answer: print the values to find it.
To run a recipe, write its name, then `()`. `say_hi()` runs its steps once. With no `()`, nothing runs.
One small task in an exercise. It turns green when your code does it.
The `:` mark at the end of an `if`, `elif` or `else` line. As in English, a colon says: here comes the list. Here, the list is the indented lines under it.
A note for people: a line that starts with `#` (Shift+3). Python skips it, the way actors skip saying the stage directions in a play script.
A yes-or-no question about two values, like `owls > wolves`. The signs are `<` `>` `<=` `>=` `==` `!=`, much like the signs in math class. Python answers `True` or `False`.
The space under your code where Python's answers appear: what `print` shows, and the error box when Python stops.
A number with a decimal point, like `24.0` or `42.5`, as in math class. Dividing with `/` always gives one.
The word that starts a recipe: `def`, the recipe's name, parentheses `( )` and a colon. The steps go under it, indented. `def` never makes a box.
Python has a definition for the name: a line like `name = value` already ran. "Not defined" means Python looked for the name and found nothing, like a word missing from a glossary.
Many values, each kept under its own tag (a key), like words in the glossary of a textbook. Curly braces `{ }` hold it: a key, a colon, its value, then a comma.
Short for else, if: another question, asked only when the questions above it were `False`. Python runs the lines under the first question whose answer is `True`.
The part that runs when the `if` question was `False`. It means otherwise, and it has no question of its own.

When Python can't run a line, it stops and shows an error box in the Console. It's like a teacher's note in the margin: it points to the spot, and it isn't a grade. Read the box's title, then Python's last line. Then fix the line with that number.
Divide and keep only the whole part (floor means round down). In math class, 50 ÷ 12 = 4 R 2, and `50 // 12` gives the 4.
Join texts end to end with `+`, like a compound word: sun + flower is sunflower. Python adds no spaces, so put the spaces inside the quotes.
A line that asks a yes-or-no question, like *If it rains, take a coat.* When the answer is `True`, Python runs the indented lines under it. When it is `False`, Python skips them.
Brings in a set of tools that Python keeps on a shelf, like fetching a dice bin. `import random` brings in Python's dice.
Asks a yes-or-no question: is this value somewhere in the list? Python answers `True` or `False`.
Spaces at the start of a line. Four spaces under an `if` mean: this line belongs to the `if`, like a sub-point under a main point in an outline.
An item's place in a list. Positions count from 0, like a ruler, so `[0]` is the first item. `[-1]` counts from the end: the last item.
The error Python shows when you ask for a position the list doesn't have. A list of 7 items has positions 0 to 6, so `[7]` is out of range.
example: IndexError: list index out of range

plain: `input()` asks a question and waits for an answer. The answer always comes back as text, even a 3.
`int` is short for integer, a whole number. `int()` turns text like `"3"` into the number 3, so you can do math with it.
`==` asks whether two values are the same. `!=` asks whether they are different, like ≠ in math. One `=` does something else: it puts a value in a box. Read one `=` as *gets*.
The tag on one value in a dictionary, like the word you look up in a glossary. A key is text, so it gets quotes: `"mana"`. To read its value, put the key in square brackets.
The error Python shows when a dictionary has no key spelled exactly like the one you asked for. Check the spelling, the capitals and the spaces.
Counts the items in a list. The last position is always one less than `len()`, because positions count from 0.
Many values kept in order under one name, like a data set in math class. Square brackets hold the list, and a comma goes between each two items.
A list whose items are lists. Read it like a theater ticket: the row first, then the seat in that row: `seats[3][1]`.
A list whose items are sheets (dictionaries). Pick a sheet by its position first, then read it by key.
Another way to choose between options: `match choice:`, then one `case` line for each value. `case _:` catches anything else, like `else`.
example:
match choice:
    case "option 1":
        print("Then we leave at dawn.")
    case _:
        print("Hm.")

plain: The signs Python does math with: `+` plus, `-` minus, `*` times (×) and `/` divided by (÷). The keyboard has no × or ÷ key, so Python uses `*` and `/`.
`max()` hands back the biggest number in a list, and `min()` hands back the smallest, wherever they are. Math class calls them the maximum and the minimum.
An older word for fix: to mend a line is to fix a small mistake in it, the way you mend a small tear in a sleeve. A slip is a small mistake.
Python met a name that no line has made yet. It's like a story that says "she" but never says who she is. Check for a typo, a capital letter, missing quotes, or a box used before it is made.
example:
print(Gold)
NameError: name 'Gold' is not defined

plain: A sheet (a dictionary) kept as a value inside another sheet. Read it with two keys in a row: the outer key first, then the inner key.
Python's word for nothing. It is not 0. A recipe with no `return` line hands back `None`.
Flips a yes-or-no answer. `not True` is `False`, and `not False` is `True`.
`in` asks a yes-or-no question: is this key in the dictionary? Python answers `True` or `False`. `not in` asks the opposite: is it missing? Both look at the keys only, never the values.
An amount Python can do math with, like points in a game. Numbers get no quotes: `3` is a number, and `"3"` is text.
Joins two yes-or-no questions. The answer is `True` when at least one answer is `True`, and also when both are.
The order Python does math in: PEMDAS, as in math class. Parentheses first, then `**`, then `*` `/` `//` `%`, then `+` and `-`, so `2 + 3 * 4` is 14.
What your program shows on the screen when it runs.
Two lists that line up, like the two columns of a table in math class: item 0 of one goes with item 0 of the other, and so on. When you change one, change the other the same way.
An ingredient: a named blank in the parentheses on the `def` line, like the x in f(x). Each call fills it with a value.
The marks `(` and `)`, the same marks you use in math class. They come in pairs: `print` keeps what it shows between them.
A line that does nothing. A recipe needs at least one line inside it, so `pass` holds the spot, like a blank recipe card, until you write a real step.
A stand-in value, like a `0` in the code you start with. It holds the place until you put the real number there.
A number multiplied by itself, like 2³ in math class. In Python, `2 ** 3` means 2 × 2 × 2, which is 8.
Shows something on the screen, in the Console under your code. In Python, print means show on the screen, not print on paper.
The question `input()` shows before it waits for an answer, like `"Who goes there? "`.
The marks `"` or `'` around text. They come in pairs, one before and one after, like quotation marks around someone's exact words in English class.
Rolls a fair die: `random.randint(1, 6)` gives any whole number from 1 to 6. Both ends are included, so 1 and 6 can come up.
Counts from a start number and stops before the stop number: `range(1, 7)` gives 1 to 6. `list(range(1, 7))` turns the count into a list.
A set of steps with a name, made with `def`. Python calls it a function. Making it runs nothing: calling its name with `()` runs the steps.
What is left over after dividing. In 50 ÷ 12 = 4 R 2, the remainder is 2, and `50 % 12` gives it. Here `%` is not percent.
Hands a value back to the line that called the recipe, and ends the recipe. Catch it in a box, or it's gone: `six = double(3)`.
Tell Python to do your code, from the top line down. Press ▶ Run, just above your code, as often as you like: running unfinished code is fine.

Write the math with box names, like `area = length * width`, instead of typing the answer, the way math class asks you to show your work. Then, when a box changes and you press Run again, the answer changes to match.
A copy of part of a list, like an excerpt from a poem. `[2:5]` copies positions 2, 3 and 4: the end is left out, and the list itself doesn't change.
`sorted(marks)` hands back a sorted copy, smallest first, and leaves `marks` as it is. `marks.sort()` sorts the list itself and hands back nothing.
`*` with text and a number repeats the text, like pressing a stamp that many times. In math, 3 × 4 means 4 + 4 + 4, and `"█" * 3` means `"█" + "█" + "█"`: `███`.
`str` is short for string, Python's word for text. `str(26)` gives the text `"26"`, which can be glued to other text.
Text inside quotes: letters, digits, spaces or marks, strung together like beads on a string. Python shows it exactly as you typed it.
Adds up every number in a list and hands back the total.
A line Python can't read. *Syntax* is how a line is put together, like grammar in English class. A missing quote, parenthesis or colon stops everything until you fix it.
Python's full message when your code stops, under Show Python's full message. Its last line gives the error's name and what went wrong. A line above it gives the line number where Python stopped.
example:
File "main.py", line 3
NameError: name 'lantren' is not defined

plain: Three quote marks in a row, `"""`. They start text that can go over many lines, and three more end it, the way a poem keeps its line breaks.
Python's words for yes and no. They start with a capital letter and have no quotes. Python answers a question like `6 > 15` with one of them.
A few values that stay together, in order, like a point (3, 8) in math class. It uses parentheses `( )`, and you read it like a list, but you can't change it.
Two values that don't fit together, like adding 5 meters to 3 seconds in math. Most often it is text glued to a number. Turn the number into text with `str()`, or take the quotes off the number.
example:
print("Gold: " + 7)
TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str

plain: What goes in a box: text in quotes, like `"Lucky"`, or a number, like `26`.
The error Python shows when a value is the right kind but can't be used here. With lists, it usually means `.remove()` was asked for a value that isn't in the list.
example:
[48, 47].remove(99)
ValueError: list.remove(x): x not in list

plain: A box with a name on it and a value inside. It's like x in math, but you pick the name, and `name = value` makes one.
A tool that pairs up two lists like the teeth of a zipper: first with first, second with second. Put it inside `list()` to see the pairs, each one a tuple.
